bib.title: Language Quantized AutoEncoders: Towards Unsupervised Text-Image Alignment

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Language Quantized AutoEncoders: Towards Unsupervised Text-Image Alignment. Hao Liu, Wilson Yan, Pieter Abbeel (UC Berkeley). Preprint, "Under review", arXiv:2302.00902v2, 3 Feb 2023.

COVERAGE: 13 of 13 pages; all 44488 chars extracted and read (body, Table 1-3, limitations, refs skimmed, Appendix A and B). Table 3 extraction is partly scrambled (see PROBLEMS). Figures 4 and 5 are bar/line plots with no numeric labels in the text. I did not run figures.py.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: LQAE turns an image into 256 text tokens by nearest-neighbour quantizing ViT patch embeddings onto the frozen RoBERTa word-embedding codebook. No image-text pairs are used.
  number: 16x16 = 256 tokens per image
  setup: 256x256 images, ViT-base encoder and decoder, patch 16x16, RoBERTa-base codebook, trained on ImageNet
  quote: "We encode each image as 16× 16 = 256 image embeddings, and vector quantize each image embedding to its nearest neighbor in the pretrained word embedding codebook."
  where: p.2 (intro); p.6 (5.1)
- claim: On 2-way open-ended miniImageNet, LQAE with text-davinci-003 reaches 53.97 average accuracy. This beats Frozen (51.3, trained on 3M caption pairs), MAE+Linear (11.71) and the ASCII baseline (4.59).
  number: 53.97 vs 51.3 vs 11.71 vs 4.59 (2-way avg); chance 50% by the paper's own caption
  setup: Real-Name Open-Ended miniImageNet; 7 settings (task induction; inner shots 1/1/3/5; repeats 0/0/0/0/1/3/5); LQAE prompted via text-davinci-003; Frozen uses a ~6B LM
  quote: "LQAE (ours) 1.5 35.2 68.2 69.8 68.5 68.7 65.9 53.97"
  where: Table 1, p.5
- claim: On 5-way, LQAE averages 29.04 against Frozen's 26.26, MAE+Linear's 2.6 and untrained LQAE's 1.63.
  number: 29.04 vs 26.26 (5-way avg)
  setup: same as above; the 5-way caption says "20% accuracy" but also says "two class labels" (copy error in the paper)
  quote: "LQAE 1 15.7 35.9 36.5 31.9 36.4 45.9 29.04"
  where: Table 2, p.5
- claim: The authors attribute part of the Frozen gap to a bigger LM, and say fine-tuning a GPT-3.5-scale model as Frozen does would be too costly.
  number: none
  setup: LQAE uses GPT-3.5, Frozen a ~6B model
  quote: "We believe this can be partially attributed to us-ing a larger language model (GPT-3.5) compared to Frozen."
  where: p.5
- claim: Replacing the learned VQ-VAE tokens with RoBERTa codebook codes drops few-shot accuracy to near zero. So GPT is using structure in the learned text, not just correlated codes.
  number: 3.24 (2-way) and 0.00 (5-way) for the VQ-to-RoBERTa mapping, vs 53.97 / 29.04 for default
  setup: Table 3 row (I), Davinci 175B
  quote: "(I) VQ to Roberta (Davinci) N/A 3.24 0.00"
  where: Table 3, p.6; text p.7
- claim: A pretrained RoBERTa is essential. A random-init LM gives near-chance few-shot results.
  number: 1.03 (2-way avg), 0.51 (5-way avg); linear 11.80
  setup: Table 3 row (B), "Trained BERT" false; extraction scrambled, my reading of the columns
  quote: "(B) false 11.80 1.03 0.51"
  where: Table 3, p.6; text p.7
- claim: Few-shot accuracy depends on mask ratio. Normal BERT masks 15%. LQAE works best near 50%, and the paper says a higher-than-normal ratio is necessary.
  number: ~50% best (plot shows 0/25/50/75% only; no numbers in text)
  setup: Fig. 5 sweep, linear ImageNet and 2-way/5-way few-shot
  quote: "standard language denoisers such as BERT commonly use a masking ratio of 15%, where LQAE performance is highest at around 50% masking ratio."
  where: p.7
- claim: Keeping only the first 75% of the 256 tokens still works well. At 50% or fewer, performance falls sharply, which suggests redundancy among the tokens.
  number: 2-way avg 50.56 (75%), 21.00 (50%), 15.45 (25%); 5-way 20.85, 5.56, 1.45
  setup: Table 3 row (G), Davinci; tokens truncated by keeping the first k%
  quote: "75 N/A 50.56 20.85"
  where: Table 3, p.6; text p.7
- claim: Larger GPT-3 models do better. With the 6.7B model, LQAE is competitive with Frozen, which also uses a 6B model.
  number: Curie 6.7B 46.55 / 22.80; Babbage 1.3B 23.85 / 14.70; Davinci 175B 53.97 / 29.04
  setup: Table 3 row (H). Column alignment is scrambled in the extraction, so the Curie/Babbage numbers are my best reading.
  quote: "(H) Curie(6.7B) N/A 46.55 22.80Babbage(1.3B) N/A 23.85 14.70"
  where: Table 3, p.6
- claim: Linear probe of intermediate RoBERTa features on LQAE tokens, trained on ImageNet, gets 35.60% for the default model. Its bar in Fig. 4 beats the VQ-VAE encoder features. The text gives no VQ-VAE number.
  number: 35.60 (linear acc, default)
  setup: ImageNet linear classification; VQ-VAE features are replicated to match the parameter count
  quote: "Default 0.0 true true 0.001 false 100 Davinci (175B) 35.60 53.97 29.04"
  where: Table 3, p.6; Fig. 4, p.5
- claim: Ablations. Removing L2 normalization before the nearest-neighbour lookup hurts. Entropy regularization does not help. A larger BERT-loss weight helps linear accuracy but hurts few-shot. Dropping the BERT loss costs very little. Quantizing before the decoder gives no benefit.
  number: no L2 norm: 30.30 / 52.45 / 27.42; BERT-loss weight 1.00: linear 36.90, 2-way 40.45, 5-way 20.93; entropy 0.5: 30.70 / 50.45 / 26.54
  setup: Table 3 rows A, D, E, F (partly scrambled)
  quote: "We observe that using larger BERT loss weight improves linear classiﬁcation but hurts few-shot classiﬁcation."
  where: p.6-7
- claim: The output text is unreadable to humans, yet an LLM can use it for few-shot learning. The authors link this to work showing few-shot learning relies on format and pattern, not exact semantics.
  number: none
  setup: Appendix A shows an ImageNet image decoded to a long token string ("Butterfly UK tobacco PE appraisal...")
  quote: "Interestingly while our model generated text outputs are not interpretable to human, large language models like GPT-3.5 can successfully do few-shot learning from them."
  where: p.6; Appendix A, p.11-12
- claim: Training recipe and loss. Loss is L2 reconstruction + β commitment + α BERT log-likelihood. The codebook loss is dropped because the codebook is frozen. Only the image encoder and decoder are trained.
  number: α=0.001, β=0.005; Adam, peak lr 1.5e-4, weight decay 0.0005; 100 epochs, 5 warmup; batch 512; 128 TPU-v3
  setup: ImageNet, RoBERTa-base frozen
  quote: "L =‖x− ˆx‖22 +β‖h− sg(z)‖22 +α logp(z|zm), whereα andβ are hyperparameters. α = 0.001 andβ = 0.005 are used as default unless otherwise mentioned."
  where: p.3-4 (3.2); p.4-5 (5.1)
- claim: The decoder gets RoBERTa's predicted output embeddings after masking (activations before logits), not the quantized codes. This pushes the encoder toward text-like codes.
  number: none
  setup: method design
  quote: "The resulting output embeddings (activations before logits) are then fed into the decoderD (not the original text encodings)."
  where: p.3
- claim: Prompt format for few-shot classification. Image tokens are interleaved with class-name text, with a task-induction line. Terms are defined as ways, inner-shots and repeats. At most 5 aligned pairs are used at test time.
  number: at most 5 aligned pairs
  setup: Fig. 3 and Section 4
  quote: "At most 5 aligned pairs are provided in each test-time example to measure few-shot learning."
  where: p.4-5
- claim: The ASCII baseline is limited to 64x64 because 256x256 would give prompts tens of thousands of tokens long, beyond GPT-3's context.
  number: 64x64
  setup: baseline
  quote: "We do not use 256× 256 resolution for this baseline is because the resulting few-shot ASCII codes are tens of thousands long that GPT-3 does not support."
  where: p.5
- claim: Mini-ImageNet eval protocol follows Frozen. It uses the Ravi & Larochelle class subset, validation-set images only, and the label is the first ImageNet class name.
  number: none
  setup: Appendix B
  quote: "All of the images used come from the validation set of ImageNet."
  where: Appendix B, p.13

LIMITS
- Authors concede there is no guarantee of human-interpretable alignment. Text may not be readable, which they say matters for domains such as healthcare. Alignment is only "realigned" through the few-shot true pairs given to GPT.
- Authors concede compute limits stopped them scaling the image encoder/decoder or the BERT-like model. They hypothesize that scaling both will help, with no evidence.
- The paper itself says "LQAE is far from state-of-the-arts". Only classification is shown. There is no VQA, captioning, robotics or generation, even though the abstract and intro motivate those.
- The comparison to Frozen mixes LM sizes (GPT-3.5 vs ~6B). Only the 6.7B Curie row is a like-for-like check, and it shows "competitive".
- The evaluation is on ImageNet-derived data and the encoder is also trained on ImageNet, so there is no out-of-distribution test.
- The claim of generalizing to arbitrary modality pairs is untested.
- Dated: relies on text-davinci-003, GPT-3/3.5 and RoBERTa-base. Later work trained on aligned pairs (CLIP-style/projector VLMs) is not compared. Reported only through Feb 2023.
- Paper-internal faults: the Table 2 caption says "two class labels ... 20%"; a Table 3 row is labelled "Davinci" for row I.

BUILDS ON: VQ-VAE (Van Den Oord et al., 2017; printed "VQAE" once); BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019); ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020); Frozen (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021) for the eval protocol and baseline; mini-ImageNet (Vinyals et al., 2016; Ravi & Larochelle, 2016); GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) and InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022); L2-normalized codes (Yu et al., 2021); MAE as baseline; CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) cited as aligned-data contrast; Min et al. 2022, Lampinen et al. 2022 and Webson & Pavlick 2021 on few-shot relying on format.

CODE: none in the paper. The loss formula above is the only formal snippet.

FIGURES (captions verbatim from extraction; no figures.py run)
- Fig. 2, p.3: "Model architecture of Language Quantization AutoEncoder (LQAE). Image is encoded to a sequence of embeddings, then vector quantized using RoBERTa codebook, followed by a high ratio masking and a frozen RoBERTa prediction, followed by a image decoder for image reconstruction." Best figure for the pipeline: encoder, frozen-codebook quantization, mask, frozen RoBERTa, decoder.
- Fig. 1, p.2: LQAE image tokens interleaved with "This is golden retriever / school bus" in a GPT-3 few-shot prompt. This shows the interface in one picture.
- Fig. 3, p.4: terminology for ways, inner-shots, repeats, task induction. Useful for explaining the eval setup.
- Fig. 5, p.7: "High mask ratio is crucial for LQAE results." Linear and few-shot accuracy against mask ratio 0/25/50/75%.
- Fig. 4, p.5: linear classification on ImageNet, VQ-VAE encoder vs LQAE variants vs random encoder.
- Fig. 6, Appendix A, p.11-12: examples of image to token string to reconstruction. It shows the output is gibberish text. The extracted images are not readable here.

PROBLEMS
- Table 3 extraction is scrambled. Rows E, G and H have misaligned columns, so I read them by position, and the values at rows E, G and H are my best reading, not certain. Re-check against the PDF page 6 before citing exact cells.
- Fig. 4 and 5 values are not in the text, so there are no numbers for them.
- Appendix A holds noisy token strings (real output, not instructions). I found no embedded instructions in the PDF.
- The Appendix B step list ends mid-list (step 4 is the last extracted).
